info.title: DIPSAC API
info.description:
File conversion, compression and SEO tooling over HTTP.

## Authentication

Every request needs your key in the `X-API-Key` header. Keys are issued from
the dashboard and start with `dps_`.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.dipsac.com/v1/pdf/merge \
  -H "X-API-Key: dps_your_key_here" \
  -F "files=@a.pdf" -F "files=@b.pdf" \
  -o merged.pdf
```

## Versioning

Everything under `/v1` is stable: parameters will not be removed and response
shapes will not change incompatibly. New optional parameters and new fields may
be added, so parse responses leniently. Breaking changes ship as `/v2`, and
`/v1` keeps working.

## Limits

Both are set by your plan and reported on every response:

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `X-RateLimit-Limit` | requests included this month (`-1` = unlimited) |
| `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | how many are left |
| `X-Plan` | the plan this key is on |

Requests-per-second and maximum upload size are also per-plan. Going over gets
`429 rate_limited` (with `Retry-After`) or `413 payload_too_large`. Requests
that fail with `404` or `5xx` are not counted against your monthly quota.

## Errors

Every failure has the same shape, so you can branch on `error` rather than
parsing prose:

```json
{
  "error": "payload_too_large",
  "message": "Upload is 82.4 MB; this key's plan allows 50 MB per request.",
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab77e0d4c31"
}
```

`request_id` is on every response in the `X-Request-Id` header too. Quote it in
support requests — it finds the exact request in our logs.

## Long-running work

Video and large PDF jobs can outlive an HTTP request. Send `mode=async` and the
call returns `202` with a job id instead of the file; poll `GET /v1/jobs/{id}`
until `status` is `succeeded`, then download from `result_url`.

post.summary: Hash a password with bcrypt
post.description:
The cost is the whole point of bcrypt, so it is a parameter rather than a
constant. Note that it is exponential: `rounds=16` is 16x the CPU of
`rounds=12` and takes a noticeable fraction of a second.

post.summary: Check a password against a bcrypt hash
post.description:
A malformed hash is `matches: false`, not an error — telling the caller
which of the two inputs was wrong is exactly what an attacker wants.

post.summary: Validate, format or minify JSON
post.description:
A syntax error comes back as `valid: false` with the line and column, and
HTTP 200 — the request itself was well-formed, and "this document is
invalid" is the answer, not a failure to answer.

get.summary: Every limit of the GLB routes
get.description:
The numbers the three routes below hold a request to: the largest scene
description, how many operations one edit may carry, how many images and of
what size, how long one request may run. Read it once and check before you
send; the numbers can change without a new version of this API.

403.description: `upgrade_required`: this key's plan does not carry the GLB API. The body names `current_plan` and `required_plan`. Not counted against the key.

post.summary: What a .glb is, and what may be done to it
post.description:
Send the model's **head** and its size; the model itself is never sent.

Answers the scene (nodes, meshes, materials, images, animations), where the
bytes go, the file's own faults (`problems`) and, under `can`, which edits
this file permits and why any of them is refused. Ask before you offer an
edit: what `can` refuses here, `POST /v1/glb/plan` refuses by the same name.

A value the head cannot answer (a picture's pixels, an animation's length)
is `null`, never 0.

head.description: The first bytes of the .glb, as a file part: its 12-byte header, its JSON chunk, and the 8-byte header of the chunk after it. That is `file.slice(0, 20 + jsonLength + 8)`, where jsonLength is the little-endian uint32 at byte 12. Never the whole file.

size.description: The length of the whole .glb in bytes.

403.description: `upgrade_required`: this key's plan does not carry the GLB API. The body names `current_plan` and `required_plan`. Not counted against the key.

411.description: `length_required`: send the form with a Content-Length header, and not in chunks.

413.description: The request, or one part of it, is larger than this step takes. `GET /v1/glb/limits` answers every limit.

422.description: A named refusal: `error` to branch on, `message` to show.

503.description: `glb_busy`: every slot is taken. `retry_after` is in seconds. Not counted against the key.

post.summary: Compile edits to a .glb into a plan of byte ranges
post.description:
Answers `{"segments": [...], "total": N, "report": {...}}`. **You build the
edited file** by concatenating the segments in order:

- `bytes`: bytes this API made, as base64 (`b64`)
- `file`: `length` bytes of the original file from `offset`
- `part`: `length` bytes of an image you sent, by its filename, from `offset`
- `zeros`: `length` zero bytes

The result is `total` bytes long. `"mode": "check"` answers the same report
without the segments, so a screen can say what an edit will do before the
images for it are sent.

`"removal": "required"` means what was removed is gone from the file, bytes
included, or the request is refused by name. `"unlink"` hides it and the
report says what stayed.

head.description: The first bytes of the .glb, as a file part: its 12-byte header, its JSON chunk, and the 8-byte header of the chunk after it. That is `file.slice(0, 20 + jsonLength + 8)`, where jsonLength is the little-endian uint32 at byte 12. Never the whole file.

size.description: The length of the whole .glb in bytes.

edit.description: JSON: `{"ops": [...], "cleanup": {...}, "removal": "required" | "unlink", "mode": "plan" | "check"}`. An operation names things by their index in the file as it arrived.

images.description: PNG or JPEG file parts an operation puts into the model. Each part's FILENAME is the name an operation refers to it by.

hashes.description: JSON `{"<image index>": "<sha-256, 64 lowercase hex>"}`, each computed by the caller over the image's own bytes. Needed only when `cleanup.dedupe` is asked for.

post.summary: Shrink one texture
post.description:
A smaller picture comes back as bytes (`image/png` or `image/jpeg`) with
`X-Glb-*` headers saying what was done. A picture that was left alone comes
back as JSON, `{"changed": false, "outcome": "..."}`, with one word saying
why. The ranges `max_size` and `jpeg_quality` may take are in
`GET /v1/glb/limits`.

max_size.description: The longest side, in pixels, of the picture that comes back.

jpeg_quality.description: The quality a JPEG is written at.

to_jpeg.description: Allow a PNG with no transparency to come back as a JPEG. Only where inspect says `jpeg_allowed` for that image.

get.summary: Check the status of an async job
get.description:
Poll this until `status` is `succeeded` or `failed`. A second or two between
polls is plenty; the work is measured in seconds, not milliseconds.

Whether the studio can be offered, and what this ACCOUNT has left.

One call, because the studio needs availability, the trial counter and the
volume allowance to render a single bar, and asking separately means the
number and the button can disagree on screen.

The price list for THIS visitor, in their currency — and what each plan
actually does.

Public — no session. Somebody deciding whether to sign up has not signed up
yet, and a pricing endpoint that requires an account is a pricing page
nobody reaching for their wallet can read. It is the one thing under /ai
that does not need a user, and it exposes nothing about one.

EVERY PLAN NOW CARRIES AN `ai` BLOCK, and that is what makes the card
honest. This answered with money alone, so components/studio/Studio.jsx
wrote Number(200000), "5 hours of transcription" and "files up to 2 hours"
into the paywall as literals — numbers that stayed put while
app/core/aitiers.py moved underneath them, which is how somebody buys a
plan that does not do what the card said. The block is DERIVED from the
tier table on every call (app/core/geopricing.ai_limits_for), so there is
nothing here to keep in sync and nothing to forget.

NOTHING IN THE RESPONSE DEPENDS ON WHO IS ASKING, and it must stay that
way. These are the same limits for everybody; what a particular caller has
LEFT is /ai/status, which requires a session precisely because that answer
is about a person. The `anon` tier is likewise not a plan and is not listed
here — a signed-out visitor is told their own allowance by /ai/status.

The studio voices, ordered for the language being generated.

Behind auth like everything else here: the list is not a secret, but a
signed-out visitor has nothing to do with it, and one public endpoint under
/ai is one more thing to remember when reasoning about what is free.

The ORDER is the product. 58 unfamiliar names alphabetically is not a choice
anybody can make; best-first for the language they picked is. See
app/core/aivoices.py for how the Hindi order was measured rather than
guessed.

Audio or video -> SRT/VTT.

post.summary: Speak
post.description:
Text -> WAV, or a job id when async=true.

TWO voice parameters, because they are two different products and the
difference is what you pay for:

    voice          one of the model's 58 STUDIO speakers, free on every
                   tier — the picker the studio renders. Forwarded by name;
                   the GPU service validates it against its own list, so an
                   unknown name comes back as its clear 400 rather than
                   being re-validated here against a copy that would go
                   stale.

    cloned_voice   a voice THIS user saved, namespaced u<id>__ so one
                   customer can never speak in another's. Paid: this is the
                   voice_cloning feature.

An earlier version had one parameter doing both jobs and got both wrong:
every studio pick was gated behind the paid feature (so a trial user's
FIRST generate answered 402), and the name was then u<id>__-prefixed and
sent as a reference wav the GPU service had never heard of. The studio's
core loop — pick a voice, hear it — was broken for exactly the people the
trial exists to convince.

get.description:
How a background /speak is getting on.

THE AUDIO IS NOT HERE, and that is the point. A finished job answers with a
`generation_id`, and the bytes come from /ai/library/{id}/audio — which
already streams, already transcodes to mp3, already enforces retention and
already checks ownership. Serving them from here would be a second
implementation of all four.

POLLED, NOT PUSHED. A websocket for a thing that finishes once, in a couple
of minutes, on a box that runs one job at a time, would be a connection to
keep alive for every waiting tab and a second delivery path to keep
working. A GET every few seconds costs one indexed row read.

delete.description: Remove one entry. The file goes too, unless another entry shares it.

get.description:
Replay a generation's audio, optionally transcoded.

?format=mp3 IS WHY THE DOWNLOAD BUTTON IS FREE. The studio holds the WAV in
memory and can save it without asking us anything; MP3 needs ffmpeg, and
the obvious place to put that — a second POST to /ai/speak — would spend a
whole generation to change a container. Here it costs nothing: the audio
already exists, this route already authenticates and scopes it, and no
meter is touched.

NOT CACHED IMMUTABLY, unlike the avatar route this otherwise resembles. The
URL here is keyed on the GENERATION, not on the content hash, and a
generation's audio can go away when its retention expires — so a year-long
immutable cache would keep serving a clip we have promised to have deleted.
aistorage.url() exists for the content-addressed form and is what a future
/ai/assets route would use.

This caller's cloned voices.

READ FROM OUR OWN REGISTRY, NOT FROM THE GPU BOX. It used to list the remote
store and filter by the `u<id>__` prefix, which worked and told us almost
nothing: no consent record, no created date, no way to show a voice whose
erasure is still in flight, and — the one that mattered — no way to answer
at all when the render node was down or had been rebuilt. A customer's
voices are a fact about their account, not about whether a GPU is awake.

The remote list is still consulted, for exactly one thing: to say whether
each voice is USABLE right now. A row whose file the node has lost is one
somebody needs told about, and silently offering it would produce a 400
from the far end at generate time with nothing to explain it.

post.summary: Register Voice
post.description:
Store a reference voice for cloning. PAID, and account-only.

Account-only is not an upsell here: a voice belongs to somebody, and an
anonymous upload could not be deleted on request by the person it belongs
to. Cloning a voice is also the one capability here that can be used
against a third party, and an audit trail with no account behind it is not
one.

delete.description:
Erase a cloned voice. THE PROMISE THIS KEEPS HAD NO IMPLEMENTATION.

POST /voices' docstring has argued since it shipped that registration is
account-only so "a voice belongs to somebody, and an anonymous upload could
not be deleted on request by the person it belongs to". Nothing deleted one.
A voice print is biometric-adjacent and DPDP §12 / GDPR Art. 17 are not
aspirational, so the gap between the sentence and the code was the sentence
being false.

WHAT HAPPENS, IN THIS ORDER, AND WHY IT IS NOT ONE STEP
  1. the row goes to `deleting` and records WHEN they asked. This survives
     everything below it failing, and it is what the reconciler looks for.
     From this moment the voice does not list and cannot be selected.
  2. the render node is asked to erase its copy.
  3. ONLY IF IT CONFIRMS: the row becomes a tombstone and our own copy —
     the reference recording — is erased with it.

STEP 3 IS ONE STEP AND NOT TWO, AND THE ORDER INSIDE IT IS DELIBERATE. The
reference recording is the ONLY thing that could ever re-register this voice
on the node. Erasing it while the node still holds its copy would leave the
two sides permanently unable to agree: we could not push the voice back, and
we could not prove what the node was holding. So a request the node did not
answer keeps its reference and stays `deleting` for the beat to retry.

So the response tells the truth in both cases rather than claiming a
completion it cannot see. A remote failure is NOT an error here: from the
customer's side the voice is gone — it no longer lists, it cannot be
selected, and nothing can synthesise with it — and reporting a 500 about a
request that has already had its visible effect is how somebody presses
delete four more times.
